lines.note: Continues the divided example from the preceding page: torishitatamuru here concerns folding, closing, or arranging a letter. The opening miuo belongs to the carried-over Japanese phrase, not a new headword.
Completes the preceding Portuguese list with arranging the letters. Concertar is retained in its historical sense of putting in order.
Torishizume means to calm or pacify; the principal parts and the repeated example below support the doubled zz. The visible terminal mark divides apaziguar across the row break.
Ziguar completes apaziguar. Kokoro wo torishizumuru illustrates calming the heart, and the Portuguese Aquietar is itself divided after its initial A.
Completes Aquietar o coração, the direct rendering of the Japanese example above. The accent and cedilla in coração are preserved.
Toriyari denotes giving and taking or exchange. Vt is italic in the explanatory apparatus; the repeated noun begins the example continued on the next row.

runs.text: Mãdar, ou dar, & receber entre ſi.

lines.note: Toriyari wo suru is explained as sending or giving and receiving between people. Mãdar retains its abbreviation tilde, and the Japanese verb has a long initial s.
Toriye here means an occasion, excuse, or pretext. The scan shows continuous Occaſião, correcting the spurious OCR division O ccaſião; kore wo begins the illustrative phrase.
Kore wo toriye ni shite means taking this as an occasion or pretext. The Portuguese translation confirms the construction; no modern segmentation is inserted into the printed Japanese.
Toriyose and toriyosuru describe bringing something near oneself or having it brought. The historical principal part ſuru is retained, and fa- continues as fazer below.
Completes fazer trazer perto de si: having something brought close. This is the causative alternative to drawing it near oneself on the preceding row.
Torizakana is appetizing food taken with drink. The negative não leads into the qualification about seasoning and sauce on the next row.

runs.text: he temperado, nem com molho pera ſobre elle

lines.note: The food is described as unseasoned and without sauce, to drink wine upon or with it. The scan supports ſobre rather than OCR ſabre.
Beber vinho completes the preceding description of food eaten with wine. It remains a separate short physical continuation.

Tooroo is equated with kamakiri, the praying mantis. The Portuguese insect name is read Bicho da saude: its capital B is damaged and E-like, so this remains a qualified reading supported by the surviving strokes and bichinho below. The headword and example carry carons; the example begins across the row break.

runs.text: rǒga vonouo aguete riù xani mucǒga go-

lines.note: The mantis raises its axe and faces the oncoming vehicle, beginning the proverbial comparison completed below. The abraded vehicle expression is read riù xani, preserving the visible separation and grave-like long-u mark; the reading of that worn vowel remains less secure than the surrounding words.

runs.text: Como eſte bichinho que aleuantando as

lines.note: Toxi completes gotoshi, like or as. The Portuguese starts to explain the little insect raising its forelegs, matching the figurative axe of the Japanese example.

runs.text: mãos ſe poẽ contra o carro que vailigeiro pera

lines.note: The insect raises its hands against a swiftly moving cart. The historical poẽ and close vailigeiro spacing are retained as printed rather than modernized.

runs.text: o deter: acommodaſe aos que compoucas forças

lines.note: The insect attempts to stop the cart; the proverb is applied to those with little strength. Compoucas is visibly close-set and is retained without silently regularizing its spacing.

runs.text: ſe querem tom arcom os muito poderoſos.

lines.note: Completes the proverb: weak people attempting to contend with the very powerful. The abraded vowel is read a in printed tom arcom; the internal separation and close joining to com are retained rather than silently regularized.
Tooro here names a lantern, distinct from the mantis entry. The printed headword carries an accent only on its first o; an expected second long-vowel mark is not supplied.
Toromen is glossed as cangas de cordão, a named corded textile. The concise historical fabric description is preserved without assigning a modern textile species.
Toroke, alternatively torake, is to melt or dissolve. The final e in Derreterſe is visible, correcting OCR Derreterſa; the alternative marker has no supplied preceding period.

runs.text: como cera, metal, &c. ou desfazerſe algũa

lines.note: The melting is illustrated with wax and metal, then with the dissolution of something soft. Metal corrects the OCR vowel, while the historical spelling and unexpanded abbreviation are retained.
Sugar supplies the example of a soft dissolving substance. Co- begins kokoro in the figurative Japanese example on the following row.
Kokoro torokuru describes the heart becoming soft or melting. The Portuguese brando makes the figurative emotional sense explicit.
The heart is dissolved like wax, completing the figurative comparison. The historical indefinite article and its tilde are retained.

runs.text: Aduer. Modo de ſe derreter, ou a-

lines.note: Tororito is an adverb for the manner of melting or softening. Aduer. belongs to the italic grammatical apparatus, and a- continues as abrandar.
Completes abrandar desta maneira and gives tororito naru, becoming soft or melted in this manner. The Japanese example ends on this physical row.
Tororo jiru is a soup made from yams and other herbs. Xiru is a Japanese noun embedded within the Portuguese explanation; its whole word is printed italic here, correcting the OCR font split after X.

runs.text: outras eruas à maneira de papas.

lines.note: Completes the soup description with other herbs prepared like a pap or porridge. The comparison describes consistency, without changing the Japanese dish name.

runs.text: Companheiros da meſma laya, ou gẽte

lines.note: Toorui denotes companions of the same kind, here a group sharing an intention. The scan reads da meſma, correcting the OCR article; gẽte remains abbreviated.

runs.text: que eſtà vnida no meſmo parecer, & vontade

lines.note: The group is united in the same opinion and will. The phrase continues the preceding definition and is completed by the purpose below.
The shared purpose is to do something bad, giving this definition of toorui a disapproving sense. The tilde in algũa is retained on u.
Tosaka and the geminated alternative tossaka name the comb of a cock or hen. The mixed long-and-short s spelling in Toſsaca is preserved.

runs.text: quer ſeja domeſtica, ou do mato.

lines.note: The comb may belong to either a domestic or a wild bird. This qualification completes the bird description rather than introducing another headword.
Tosakanori, also tossakanori, is described as a seaweed. The historical Hũs and joined domar are preserved; the following line supplies its colour and use.

runs.text: vermelhos q̃ ſe comẽ. As vezes ſe diz Toſa-

lines.note: The seaweed is red and edible. The Portuguese then introduces the shortened Japanese name Toſa-, completed by ca on the following row; the term is embedded in Portuguese explanation.
Ca completes the shortened name Tosaka. The Latin minus proprie qualifies that name as less exact, rather than supplying another botanical property.
Toosaku means this year's cultivation or sowing. The example below asks after the resulting crop or harvest.

Toosaku wa nanto gozaruka asks how this year's crop is. The scan supplies the paragraph sign and question mark omitted by OCR; the Portuguese nouidade is divided across rows and closely joined to its article.
Completes the Portuguese question about how this year's harvest is. Nouidade here concerns the crop, not merely abstract novelty.
Toosakugyoo concerns cultivating and preparing fields. The scan supports cultiuar, correcting the garbled OCR cubsiuar, and var- continues as varzeas.

runs.text: zeas no principio do ãno, ou na prima vera.

lines.note: The work is done at the beginning of the year or in spring. The written-usage label S. is upright, separate from the italic explanation; the printed prima vera spacing is retained.

runs.text: Hum certo Sacazzuqui ſobre ſua ſal-

lines.note: Toosan is a particular sakazuki cup on its tray. The embedded Japanese Sacazzuqui is printed italic with the Portuguese in this occurrence; its initial S and Portuguese ſal- correct OCR B and f confusions.

runs.text: ua de pao vruxada de vermelho.

lines.note: Ua completes ſalua, the serving tray. It is wooden and lacquered red; vruxada is the Portuguese explanation's urushi-derived adjective and remains in italic type.
Tosama or tosamano describes something in a borrowed or non-deliberate manner. The entry is aligned with the headwords, not indented as a continuation; em- continues in column 2 as emprestado.

runs.text: preſtado, ou que nãohe de propoſito.

lines.note: Completes emprestado from the bottom of column 1, then adds not deliberately or expressly. The joined nãohe is retained as visible spacing.
Tosamani is the adverb corresponding to the preceding adjective-like forms. Its short definition relies on the immediately preceding sense; Adu. remains italic.
Tosan is equated with hikidemono, a present or gift. The right edge has a full stop after dadiua, not the OCR hyphen.
Tosan wo yaru means sending or giving a present. The final r in dar is visible against the rule and restores the verb truncated by OCR.
Preſente completes both mandar and dar in the preceding translation. This short continuation is genuine body text.

Toosoo is explained by toogasa and glossed as boubas, the historical disease term. Both o vowels of the headword carry carons: after an independent reading, the supplied NINJAL index (v202510, 264d03) prompted enlargement that resolved the faint marks. The gloss is retained without replacing it with a modern diagnosis.
Tosoo has the preferred alternative Tosuu, explained as an angya no boozu, a travelling Buddhist monk. Melius corrects OCR Meltis and is italic; the Japanese explanatory forms remain upright.
The Portuguese gives the direct meaning, a pilgrim or travelling Buddhist monk. It completes the Japanese synonym on the preceding row.

Tosot names the Buddhist Tusita realm, with Tosot no naiin specifying its inner court. The scan supports no rather than OCR io; the Portuguese explanation begins its historical identification with Amida and must be retained as printed.

runs.text: mida que os Gentios imaginão auer.

lines.note: Completes Amida and the dictionary's description of a paradise imagined by the Gentios. This records the source's religious characterization without endorsing or silently correcting its identification.
Tosotten is described as the name of a heaven. The close Nomede spacing is retained rather than regularized to Nome de.
Tosuu refers back to Tosoo and gives tosuu no gyoonin, a religious practitioner on pilgrimage. The scan recovers the terminal nin and full stop lost in OCR guiǒri-; the first headword uses a short s.
The Portuguese explains the example as a Buddhist monk who travels on pilgrimage. It continues the preceding Japanese phrase.

runs.text: Secretas que eſtão da parte do Leste.

lines.note: Toosu denotes privies situated on the eastern side. Eſtão corrects the OCR eſtco, while the source's descriptive explanation is preserved.
The geminated tossaka form refers back to tosaka, the bird's comb. The two long-s types in this occurrence are retained rather than harmonized with the earlier mixed pair.
Tossakanori refers above to tosakanori, the red edible seaweed. The mixed long and short s spelling is preserved occurrence by occurrence.

Tootsuu is explained as numbing pain, shibiruru itami. Enlargement confirms a faint circumflex over o and a clear caron over u, after a comparison prompt from the supplied NINJAL index (v202510, 264d11); the Portuguese burning-pain alternative continues below.
Completes arder and adds stinging with pain. The row supplies the second half of the painful-sensation gloss, not another Japanese entry.
Totsugai, totsugoo, totsugoota names mating or copulation. The initial T of the Portuguese Terem belongs with the italic gloss rather than the Japanese headword, correcting the OCR font split.
The definition extends the same act to humans as well as animals. The horizontal abbreviation mark in homẽs is a tilde, not the OCR grave accent.
Totsugi, totsugu, totsuida supplies another verb for animals mating. The cedilla and final animaes are visible and replace the OCR plain c and terminal r.
Totsu totsuto describes acting in a hurried or flustered manner. The adverbial definition continues onto the next row.
The manner is hurried and somewhat disturbed or confused. Perturbação corrects OCR perturhação; the abbreviated tildes in apreßadamẽte and cõ are retained.
Tote is explained through to yuute, saying that. The scan reads Toyǔte without the spurious OCR i, and Mai- begins the verb mairu below.
Mairu or mairoo tote expresses saying that one would go. Iria, visible in the Portuguese, corrects the meaningless OCR tria.
A second entry describes tote grammatically as a particle related to gerund and participle constructions. The source's grammatical categories are retained rather than replaced by modern terminology.

runs.text: quando ſe ajunta à voz do futuro.

lines.note: The construction is specified as one joined to a future form and equivalent to for or in order to. The explanatory i is upright in the local type, separate from the surrounding italic Portuguese.

runs.text: ou por. Como ſe verà na Arte.

lines.note: Adds por and refers the reader to the Arte for the grammatical explanation. Arte is the Portuguese title-reference within the italic apparatus.

runs.text: Hũa pintura em que està pintada a lũa

lines.note: Tootei is a picture depicting the autumn moon. The scan shows lũa, correcting OCR Iida; the scene is geographically specified below.

runs.text: do Outono que ſe vè em hua certa parte da Chi

lines.note: The moon is seen in a particular part of China. The final Chi is divided from na on the next row, with no added hyphen at the rule.

runs.text: na, dõde he mais apraziuel, & tida por hua das

lines.note: China is completed, followed by the claim that the scene is especially pleasing and counted among a celebrated group. The scan recovers the ampersand, tida, and final das from OCR damage; dõde remains unexpanded.

Completes the description as one of the eight celebrated views in China. The initial C of the final China is abraded but its remaining curved trace supports it; the reading is consistent with the preceding geographical name.

runs.text: Adu. Aßi como aßi, ou de qual

lines.note: Totemo is explained here as anyway or in any manner. The second aßi ends in i, correcting OCR aßs; qual continues into qualquer below without supplying a hyphen.
Completes qualquer maneira and illustrates totemo narumai, saying that something will not be possible. The Portuguese begins its explanatory paraphrase on this row.

runs.text: derradeiro, ou por nenhũa via poderà ſer.

lines.note: The translation concludes with the sense that it cannot be by any means. The historical por nenhũa via construction agrees with the negative Japanese narumai without inserting a modern negative word.
Totemono koto ni introduces doing something while the occasion is available. Occa- begins the Portuguese occasion phrase continued below.

runs.text: ſião, ou ja que estais com a mão na obra, &c.

lines.note: The occasion is paraphrased as already having one's hand in the work. The explanation gives the practical while-you-are-at-it sense of the phrase.
Totemono koto ni kore wo shite kudasarei asks the listener to do this while already engaged in the work. The honorific request is divided after cudaſa-.

runs.text: Peço vos façais iſto ja que começastes a

lines.note: Rei completes kudasarei; the Portuguese asks the listener to do this now that they have begun. Façais corrects OCR fuçais, and the Japanese-ending period remains outside the italic translation.

runs.text: fazer, ou eſtais com a mão na obra, &c.

lines.note: Completes the alternative explanation: since the listener has begun doing the work or already has a hand in it. The printed word boundary after com is preserved.

Tooten is paraphrased as tenjiku ni wataru, crossing to Tenjiku. The Portuguese specifically gives Sião; this historical pairing is retained without changing either place-name. The headword vowel is e, not OCR o.

runs.text: Eſtes inimigos de agora, ou preſẽtes.

lines.note: Tooteki denotes the present or current enemies. It is an independent unindented headword, with no printed paragraph sign before it; the OCR sign is removed and the visible absence of a headword stop retained.

Totoo is explained as taitoo ni wataru, crossing to China. The medial t of the headword is heavily abraded; Totǒ and Taitǒni are the selected readings supported by residual strokes and the Japanese phrase, correcting OCR i and r. The headword remains a qualified recovery.
Tootoo, alternatively tokutoku, is glossed as quickly or early. The two adverbial alternatives and their printed accents are preserved separately from the preceding geographical entry.

runs.text: Pay. He palaura de q̃ vſão os mininos.

lines.note: Toto means father in children's speech. The Portuguese explicitly identifies the childish usage; mininos retains its historical vowel.
Totoo, or toorui, is a company of idle or disreputable people. The cross-reference's o has a caron in this occurrence, agreeing with the scan rather than OCR tôrui.
The company is disposed and united to do harm. The description continues on the bottom physical body row, which the OCR had mixed with the separate right-hand catchword.

Inſultos completes the preceding list of harmful acts. It is body text at the left of the bottom row; the separate Tǒto- at the right is a catchword anticipating the next page and is not repeated in the running text.
